title: Bats and people
teaches: The 1943 bat bomb, Austin's bridge colony, guano and gunpowder, what bats are worth to farms, and what to do about a bat in the house
summary: **The bat bomb nearly flew.** In 1943 the US military armed Mexican free-tailed bats with tiny napalm bombs, burned its own airfield by accident, and dropped the plan for the atomic bomb.
**Bats roost in crevices, and people build them.** Austin's Congress Avenue Bridge, rebuilt in 1980, now holds up to 1.5 million bats each summer.
**Fear turned to pride in Austin.** Merlin Tuttle and Bat Conservation International persuaded the city that bats left alone are harmless and eat tonnes of insects a night.
**A colony eats most once its young fly.** In late summer the colony nearly doubles, and the nightly catch peaks.
**Guano is rich in nitrogen.** Bat droppings from caves have been dug as fertiliser and, in the Civil War, boiled into saltpetre for gunpowder.
**Bats save farmers billions, by a wide estimate.** Boyles and colleagues put it at 3.7 to 53 billion dollars a year in the United States, the width itself a measure of how little is known.
**A bat in a bedroom is a call to public health.** If it may have touched anyone, or someone was asleep, keep the bat safely contained for testing; never touch it with bare hands.
**Shut bats out only when no pups are inside.** Use one-way doors in late summer or autumn, never while young bats cannot yet fly.

blocks.text: Lytle S. Adams was a dentist from Irwin, Pennsylvania, with a taste for inventions. Late in 1941 he stood at the mouth of Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico and watched hundreds of thousands of Mexican free-tailed bats pour out into the evening. A few weeks later Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. In January 1942 Adams wrote to the White House with a plan to attack Japan's cities with bats.

Before reading on, it is worth asking what Adams had seen that made bats look like a weapon. A free-tailed bat weighs about 12 g and can carry more than its own weight in food. More to the point, think about where a bat goes at dawn, and what Japanese cities of the 1940s were mostly built of.

Adams's idea was that bats released over a city at night would, as dawn came, look for places to hide: under eaves, in attics, in the gaps of walls. Japanese houses were built largely of wood and paper. If each bat carried a small firebomb on a timer, thousands of fires would start at once in places no one could see, all over the city. Roosevelt passed the letter on with a note that reportedly called it a perfectly wild idea, but worth looking into.

The work that followed, later named Project X-Ray, ran for more than two years. Louis Fieser, the Harvard chemist who had just invented napalm, designed firebombs of 17 to 28 g with a delay fuse, small enough to clip to the loose skin of a bat's chest.[^fieser] Donald Griffin, whose detector work lesson 1 followed, was brought in as an adviser. The bats were cooled into torpor, the same state as lesson 7's hibernating bats, so they could be handled and packed: over a thousand bats in trays inside a bomb casing that would open on a parachute over its target.

On 15 May 1943, at an auxiliary base of the Carlsbad Army Airfield, some armed bats got loose before anyone could stop them. They did exactly what Adams had predicted, and roosted in the nearest buildings, under a fuel tank among them. The fires burned much of the test range.[^general] Later in 1943 the Navy took over, then the Marines, and in a test at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah bats set a mock Japanese village alight. But the project would not be ready for battle before the middle of 1945, and in 1944 Admiral Ernest King cancelled it. In August 1945 the war ended with the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

blocks.text: Mexican free-tailed bats roost in great crowds in caves across Texas and northern Mexico, and they will take any dark, narrow crevice that stays warm. In 1980 the city of Austin rebuilt the deck of the Congress Avenue Bridge over the Colorado River in the middle of town. Underneath, the new concrete left long slots between the beams, a couple of centimetres wide and some 40 cm deep. To a free-tailed bat these were perfect, and within a few years the bridge held hundreds of thousands of them.

The city was alarmed. Newspapers reported bats invading Austin, people worried about rabies, and there were calls to get rid of the colony. In 1986 Merlin Tuttle, a bat biologist then at the Milwaukee Public Museum, moved his young charity, Bat Conservation International, to Austin and set about changing minds. His argument was the one in the last lesson: bats that are left alone are harmless, very few carry rabies, and the danger is only in handling one. And these bats ate insects, a great many of them, every night.[^bumsteer]

It worked. The bridge colony is now among the city's sights, with somewhere between 750,000 and 1.5 million bats each summer, and up to 100,000 people a year come to watch the emergence at dusk, a dark ribbon of bats pouring out from under the bridge and heading off over the river. Most of the bats are females. They arrive pregnant from Mexico in spring, give birth in June, raise their pups in the crevices, and leave again in autumn.

blocks.caption: The bridge colony through one season: how many bats (dashed) and how many tonnes of insects they eat a night (shaded). A model built from round numbers: free-tailed bats weigh about 12 g, and a nursing mother eats some 70% of her weight a night.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the season through its peak

blocks.text: Each nursing mother eats the most in early summer, but the colony as a whole eats most in August, when the young are flying and hunting for themselves and the number of mouths nearly doubles. In the model a full colony eats seven to nine tonnes of insects a night at its peak, close to the 10,000 to 30,000 pounds that are often quoted. Many are moths flying high over the farms of central Texas.

A big colony leaves a lot behind. **Guano**, from a Quechua word by way of Spanish, is the droppings of bats or seabirds, and in a cave used for centuries it can lie metres deep. It is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, the main things a crop needs from a fertiliser, and caves such as Bracken Cave near San Antonio and Frio Cave in Uvalde County were dug for guano from the nineteenth century on, and sold to farmers.

The nitrogen in old guano has a second use. Over time it turns into nitrates, salts that dissolve in water. Soaked out of guano or cave earth and boiled with wood ash, they give saltpetre, potassium nitrate, which is three quarters of black gunpowder by weight.[^saltpetre] During the Civil War the blockaded Confederacy was short of saltpetre and mined caves across the South for it. A Texas historical marker near Concan, in Uvalde County, records Confederate gunpowder made from a bat cave's guano, and a saltpetre works near New Braunfels supplied the Confederate government.

In 2006 Cutler Cleveland and his colleagues worked out what Mexican free-tailed bats were worth to cotton farmers in eight counties of south-central Texas. The bats eat the moths of the cotton bollworm, a caterpillar that also eats corn, and by eating them they save farmers some spraying and some crop. The answer was about three quarters of a million dollars a year, between an eighth and a sixth of the value of the cotton crop in those counties.

In 2011, writing in *Science* as white-nose syndrome spread, Justin Boyles, Paul Cryan, Gary McCracken and Thomas Kunz scaled that kind of estimate up to the whole of the United States. Their figure for the value of bats to American farms was about 23 billion dollars a year, within a range from 3.7 to 53 billion. A range that wide says how much is unknown: how many insects bats eat, how many of those are pests, and how much spraying farmers would actually add without them. Even the low end is a large number, and it was the point of the paper: losing bats to white-nose would cost farmers money.

Bats find their way into houses through gaps of a centimetre or two, and a lone bat in a room at night is usually a young one that took a wrong turn. The question that matters is rabies. As the last lesson showed, a bat that ends up indoors or on the ground is more likely than most to be sick, and a bat bite can be too small to notice. So health departments count it as a possible exposure if a bat was in a room where someone was asleep, or with a small child or anyone who cannot say whether it touched them.[^pep] Then the bat should not simply be let go: if it can be caught safely, with thick gloves and a box, it can be tested, and a negative test spares a course of injections.

blocks.caption: What to do when you find a bat, after advice from US and Washington public health and wildlife agencies. When in doubt, call your local public health office.

root.ask: Could the bat have touched anyone? That includes being in a room where someone was asleep, or with a child or anyone who can't say.

choices.text: Yes, or I can't be sure
choices.name: Keep it and call public health
choices.about: Don't let it go. If it can be done safely, wearing thick leather gloves, trap it under a box or tub, slide card underneath and tape it shut. Call your local public health office: the bat can be tested. Wash any bite or scratch with soap and water for 15 minutes.

choices.name: Show it the way out
choices.about: Shut the room's inside doors, open a window or outside door wide, turn the lights off and watch quietly from outside the room. Most bats find the way out within an hour.

choices.text: On the ground or a wall outside
choices.name: Leave it and call a rehabilitator
choices.about: A bat on the ground by day may be sick, hurt or a young one that fell. Keep children and pets away, don't touch it, and call a wildlife rehabilitator or the state wildlife agency.

choices.text: A colony in the attic or walls

then.ask: What time of year is it?

choices.name: Wait until the pups fly
choices.about: There may be pups inside that cannot fly yet; shut the mothers out now and the pups starve in the walls. Wait until late summer.

choices.text: Late summer to autumn, or early spring
choices.name: Fit one-way doors, then seal
choices.about: Put one-way exits over the gaps the bats use, leave them a week, then seal every gap for good. A bat house nearby gives them somewhere else to go.

specimens.name: Keep it and call public health
specimens.hint: you wake at 3 am to a bat flying round your bedroom

specimens.name: Show it the way out
specimens.hint: a bat circles the living room at dusk while the whole family watches from the doorway

specimens.name: Leave it and call a rehabilitator
specimens.hint: a bat lies on the patio at noon in August

specimens.name: Wait until the pups fly
specimens.hint: in June you hear squeaking in the attic, and bats leave the eaves at dusk

blocks.text: A colony in an attic is a different matter. Bats in a house do no harm to people who leave them alone, but their droppings pile up and smell, and many people would rather they lived elsewhere. No poison is approved for use on bats in the United States, and poisoned bats end up on floors and in living rooms, where people and pets meet them. The method that works is exclusion: a one-way door over each gap the bats use, which lets them crawl out at dusk but not back in.

blocks.caption: Shutting bats out of a house: a one-way door of netting or tubing over the gap they use, and the months to do it in Washington.

blocks.text: Shut a maternity colony out in June or July and the pups, which cannot yet fly, are left inside to starve. In winter some bats hibernate in buildings, and a bat shut out then has nowhere to go. That leaves spring, before the pups are born, and late summer and autumn, after they fly.

blocks.caption: Five questions on bats and people
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why did Lytle Adams think bats could start fires all through a Japanese city?
choices: At dawn bats look for crevices under eaves and in attics, and the houses were largely wood and paper
Bats are drawn to light, so they would fly toward lit windows and into rooms
Bats fly in tight swarms, so a whole colony would land on one building together
items.why: A bat seeks a hidden roost as day comes. Carrying a timed firebomb, each one would start a fire in a hidden spot, and thousands would start at once.

items.ask: Why does the Congress Avenue Bridge colony eat the most insects in a night in August rather than in early summer?
choices: The young are flying and feeding by then, so the colony has nearly doubled
August nights are longer, so each bat hunts for more hours
The mothers eat most once their pups are weaned
items.why: A nursing mother eats the most each, but in August the young hunt too and the number of mouths nearly doubles.

items.ask: How did bat guano become gunpowder in the Civil War?
choices: Its nitrogen turns to nitrates, which were soaked out and boiled with wood ash into saltpetre
It was dried and burned as the fuel in black powder in place of charcoal
Its phosphorus was refined into the powder's sulphur
items.why: Black powder is about three quarters saltpetre, potassium nitrate, and old guano is a rich source of nitrates.

items.ask: A bat is found flying in a room where a child was asleep. Nobody saw a bite. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Contain the bat safely with gloves and a box, and call public health so it can be tested
Open the window and let it go, since no bite was seen
Wait to see whether the child develops symptoms over the next few weeks
items.why: Bat bites can go unnoticed, so a sleeping child counts as possibly exposed. Testing the bat decides whether treatment is needed; once rabies symptoms start it is too late.

items.ask: Why should bats be shut out of an attic in late summer or autumn rather than in June?
choices: In June there may be pups inside that cannot fly yet and would starve
Bats are more aggressive in June and harder to handle
One-way doors only work once the nights are cool
items.why: Mothers give birth in early summer and the pups fly a few weeks later. Exclude before birth or after they fly, never between.

fieser.title: Fieser and napalm
fieser.text: Louis Fieser and his group at Harvard developed napalm in 1942, a petrol thickened into a sticky gel that burns long and clings. The bat bombs were small capsules of it with a delay fuse.

general.title: The general's car
general.text: The story is often told that a general's car burned in the Carlsbad fire too. Accounts vary in the details, but all agree that the bats did to the base what they had been meant to do to Japan.

bumsteer.title: A Bum Steer
bumsteer.text: In 1986 *Texas Monthly* gave Tuttle one of its Bum Steer Awards, its yearly mockery of Texans' follies, for trying to persuade Austin to love its bats. The city now has a bat sculpture near the bridge and a bat-watching cruise on the river.

saltpetre.title: Making saltpetre
saltpetre.text: Nitrate-rich earth or guano was packed into vats and water poured through it. The liquid that ran out was mixed with lye from wood ash, which swaps its calcium for potassium, then boiled down until crystals of potassium nitrate formed. Black powder is about 75% saltpetre, 15% charcoal and 10% sulphur.

pep.title: Treatment after a bite
pep.text: Rabies treatment after a possible exposure is a dose of antibodies and a course of four vaccine injections over two weeks. It works because the virus travels slowly along nerves to the brain, giving the vaccine time to raise the body's own defences.
